criterion_notes.c1: Addresses urban water service delivery (WSD) in five utility service areas in Kenya (Old Town in Mombasa, Migosi in Kisumu, Kangemi in Nairobi) and Ghana (Madina and Nima in Accra).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — examines water governance, institutional integrity (transparency of written rules, accountability/control mechanisms, participation), corruption risks, opportunistic vs. pragmatic management practices, and public corporate utility (Kenya) vs. private sector participation (Ghana) arrangements. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: No — rather than analyzing a specific legal or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariff rules, administrative burden, or disconnection/enforcement rules), the paper models abstract behavioural corruption risks, social-network reciprocity ties, and opportunistic vs. pragmatic management across principal-agent game dyads (assigning both countries identical pragmatic/free-riding parameters at the utility-user interface).
criterion_notes.c3: No new empirical evidence or empirical analysis is conducted. The study builds and runs a deterministic exploratory agent-based simulation model (ABM) in NetLogo based on 2x2 game-theoretic social dilemmas (Prisoner's Dilemma, Snow Drift, Stag Hunt). Previously published aggregate scores from Bellaubi and Visscher (2014, 2016), GII (2011), and TIK (2011) are imported solely to parameterize and calibrate a model constant (C), with no primary data collection or empirical methodology reported.
criterion_notes.c4: Although Table 5 reprints secondary area-level benchmark scores (continuity, quality, coverage, affordability, and quantity; with continuity and coverage definitions transposed in Table 3) from Bellaubi and Visscher (2014) to calibrate the model, the analytical outcome generated and evaluated by this paper's ABM is simulated game-theoretic principal-agent payoffs summed across ministry, regulator, municipality/agency, utility, and user dyads (Table 7), not an empirically measured water access outcome.
criterion_notes.c5: Study design is identifiable as a computational agent-based simulation rather than an empirical study, but for the underlying empirical case studies no household/respondent population or sample sizes or sampling procedures are reported, and Figures 1 and 2 (containing the dyad-specific TAP and social cost input scores) are absent from the text beyond captions. In the ABM itself, all users in each country are collapsed into a single representative actor node.

evidence_quotes.quote: We explore the extent to which corruption and management practices affect the performance of WSD by developing an exploratory agent-based model (ABM) that builds on the principal-agent theory.

The ABM builds on a principal-agent representation for Kenya and Ghana WSD that results from analyzing three case studies in Kenya and two in Ghana, carried out as a part of Transparency International’s “Transparency and Integrity in Service Delivery in Africa Program” (Bellaubi and Visscher 2014).

In Kenya and Ghana, the relationship between water companies (agents) and users (principals) is characterized by low TAP and balance of power between the agent and the principal resulting in pragmatic management.
The total performance of WSD is measured as the sum of the different payoffs obtained by all the actors involved as the result of the transactions among all of them.

The ABM presented is a deterministic explanatory learning model that aims to explain how corruption risks and management practices affect WSD’s performances in Kenya and Ghana, considering the role of learning and social networks.

raw_response.exposure: Simulated corruption risks, integrity parameters (transparency, accountability, participation, and social reciprocity costs/gains), and opportunistic versus pragmatic management practices in principal-agent relationships under public utility (Kenya) and private sector participation (Ghana) water governance
raw_response.outcome: Simulated principal-agent game-theoretic strategies (cooperation/defection equilibria) and summed actor payoffs representing system-level water service delivery (WSD) performance, calibrated against secondary case-study WSDA benchmark scores
raw_response.population_and_sample: Stylized actor nodes in a NetLogo agent-based model (ministry, regulator, municipality/water agency, water utility/operator, and a single users node) calibrated to five previously published urban case-study areas in Kenya (Old Town, Migosi, Kangemi) and Ghana (Madina, Nima); empirical household/respondent sample sizes are not reported
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). This article presents a deterministic computational simulation — an exploratory agent-based model (ABM) in NetLogo simulating 2x2 game-theoretic social dilemmas (Prisoner's Dilemma, Snow Drift, Stag Hunt) among stylized sector actors. It conducts no primary empirical data collection or empirical analysis, importing aggregate summary scores from previously published case studies (Bellaubi and Visscher 2014, 2016; GII 2011; TIK 2011) solely to calibrate a model constant (C) and reporting simulated principal-agent game strategies and payoffs rather than empirical household service access outcomes. Additionally, under the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it models broad corruption risks, social-tie reciprocity, and opportunistic versus pragmatic management rather than a specific legal or administrative rule-type mechanism directly governing household water access, and does not report the underlying household population or sample.
raw_response.study_design: Computational simulation: deterministic exploratory agent-based model (ABM) calibrated with secondary case-study summary scores
